26:
The book now turns from collected messages to stories about ⟦p:jeremiah_853|Jeremiah⟧ himself, and it steps back in time to do so. This scene is set at the beginning of ⟦p:jehoiakim_1085|Jehoiakim⟧'s reign, just after ⟦p:josiah_1730|Josiah⟧'s death, and it tells what happened when Jeremiah stood in the temple court and gave the warning already heard in chapter seven: this house will become like ⟦l:shiloh_1081|Shiloh⟧.

Priests, prophets and people seize him and shout that he must die. The royal officials come up from the palace and sit in judgement at the New Gate of the temple, and the scene becomes a trial. ⟦p:jeremiah_853|Jeremiah⟧ retracts nothing, and warns his judges that if they kill him they will bring innocent blood on the city.

Some of the elders recall a precedent. A century earlier, ⟦p:micah_2053|Micah⟧ of ⟦l:moresheth_819|Moresheth⟧ had said that ⟦l:zion_1263|Zion⟧ would be ploughed like a field, and King ⟦p:hezekiah_1512|Hezekiah⟧ did not kill him, but sought the Lord. Then, to show how close ⟦p:jeremiah_853|Jeremiah⟧ came, the chapter tells of another prophet, Uriah, who spoke the same message and did not survive. Jeremiah is protected by ⟦p:ahikam_141|Ahikam⟧ son of ⟦p:shaphan_2550|Shaphan⟧. Shaphan was the royal scribe who had read the newly found book of the law to King ⟦p:josiah_1730|Josiah⟧, and his family will appear again.
27:
Some years have passed. ⟦p:jehoiakim_1085|Jehoiakim⟧ is dead, his son ⟦p:jehoiachin_791|Jeconiah⟧ is in ⟦l:babylon_151|Babylon⟧, and ⟦p:zedekiah_1950|Zedekiah⟧ reigns as ⟦p:nebuchadnezzar_2167|Nebuchadnezzar⟧'s appointee. Envoys from the kings of ⟦l:edom_357|Edom⟧, ⟦l:moab_815|Moab⟧, ⟦l:ammon_58|Ammon⟧, ⟦l:tyre_1184|Tyre⟧ and ⟦l:sidon_1093|Sidon⟧ have come to Zedekiah in ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧, and prophets in every one of these courts are promising that no one will have to serve the king of Babylon. The next chapter dates these days to Zedekiah's fourth year.

⟦p:jeremiah_853|Jeremiah⟧ is told to make a yoke of leather straps, the harness of an ox, and put it on his own neck, and to send word back to the kings by their envoys. The Lord made the earth and gives it to whom he pleases, and he has given these lands to his servant ⟦p:nebuchadnezzar_2167|Nebuchadnezzar⟧. Any nation that bows its neck to ⟦l:babylon_151|Babylon⟧ will remain in its land. Any nation that resists will be destroyed.

He says the same to ⟦p:zedekiah_1950|Zedekiah⟧, and then to the priests and people, who are hearing from other prophets that the temple treasures taken to ⟦l:babylon_151|Babylon⟧ will soon come back. ⟦p:jeremiah_853|Jeremiah⟧ answers that even the great bronze pillars and the bronze Sea still standing in the temple court will follow them.
28:
That same year, in the temple, ⟦p:jeremiah_853|Jeremiah⟧ is publicly contradicted. The challenger is ⟦p:hananiah_1395|Hananiah⟧ son of Azzur, a prophet from ⟦l:gibeon_470|Gibeon⟧, and he speaks just as Jeremiah does, in the name of the Lord of Hosts. The yoke of ⟦l:babylon_151|Babylon⟧ is broken, he says. Within two years the temple treasures will be returned, and King ⟦p:jehoiachin_791|Jeconiah⟧ and the exiles will come home.

⟦p:jeremiah_853|Jeremiah⟧'s first reply is remarkable. Amen, he says. May the Lord do so. He would like nothing better. But he reminds ⟦p:hananiah_1395|Hananiah⟧ that the prophets of old spoke of war and disaster, and that a prophet who promises peace will be known as truly sent only when his words come true.

Then ⟦p:hananiah_1395|Hananiah⟧ takes the yoke from ⟦p:jeremiah_853|Jeremiah⟧'s neck and breaks it in front of everyone, and Jeremiah simply walks away. Only later does the word of the Lord come to him, and he returns with a message for Hananiah. The chapter's ending is told in a single plain sentence.
29:
While false prophets contend with ⟦p:jeremiah_853|Jeremiah⟧ in ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧, the same struggle is going on among the exiles in ⟦l:babylon_151|Babylon⟧. Jeremiah sends them a letter, carried by two envoys whom ⟦p:zedekiah_3031|Zedekiah⟧ is sending to ⟦p:nebuchadnezzar_2167|Nebuchadnezzar⟧, one of them a son of ⟦p:shaphan_2550|Shaphan⟧.

The exiles are being told by their own prophets that their stay will be short. ⟦p:jeremiah_853|Jeremiah⟧'s letter says the opposite. Build houses and live in them. Plant gardens. Marry, and see your children married. Seek the welfare of the city where you have been sent and pray to the Lord for it, for in its welfare you will find your own. Only when ⟦l:babylon_151|Babylon⟧'s seventy years are complete will the Lord bring them home. Here is one of the most quoted promises in the book, of plans for a future and a hope, spoken to people most of whom would not live to see the return.

The letter also names false prophets among the exiles, and the chapter ends with an angry reply from one of them, ⟦p:shemaiah_2643|Shemaiah⟧, who writes back to ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧ demanding that the priests put ⟦p:jeremiah_853|Jeremiah⟧ in the stocks.
30:
After so many chapters of warning, the tone changes almost completely. ⟦p:jeremiah_853|Jeremiah⟧ is told to write in a book all the words the Lord has spoken to him, because the days are coming when the Lord will restore his people, Israel and Judah together, to the land given to their fathers. These four chapters are often called the Book of Consolation.

This chapter and the next are poetry, and undated. The sorrow is not forgotten. The poem opens with a cry of terror, a time of distress for ⟦p:israel_682|Jacob⟧ unlike any other. Judah's wound is incurable, her allies gone, her punishment deserved. Then the turn comes, from the Lord alone. I will restore your health and heal your wounds, he says, because they have called you an outcast.

The promises are concrete: the city rebuilt on its ruins, the palace in its proper place, songs of thanksgiving, children as in former days, and a ruler who comes from among the people themselves. Running through it is the covenant promise first spoken at ⟦l:sinai_1098|Sinai⟧: you will be my people, and I will be your God.
31:
The promises now reach the northern tribes, ⟦p:ephraim_1206|Ephraim⟧ and ⟦l:samaria_1022|Samaria⟧, lost to ⟦l:assyria_111|Assyria⟧ long before ⟦p:jeremiah_853|Jeremiah⟧ was born. I have loved you with an everlasting love, the Lord says. There will be vineyards on the hills of Samaria again, and watchmen on the hills of Ephraim calling the people up to ⟦l:zion_1263|Zion⟧. The blind and the lame, mothers with child, will come back from the north in a great company.

One brief passage is full of sorrow. A voice is heard in ⟦l:ramah_972|Ramah⟧, a town of ⟦p:benjamin_463|Benjamin⟧: ⟦p:rachel_2386|Rachel⟧, the mother of ⟦p:joseph_1710|Joseph⟧ and Benjamin, weeping for her children because they are no more. The Lord tells her to dry her tears, for they will return. ⟦p:matthew_1971|Matthew⟧'s Gospel would recall these words at the slaughter of the children of ⟦l:bethlehem_218|Bethlehem⟧.

Then comes the passage for which this chapter is best known. The Lord promises a new covenant, unlike the one made at the exodus, which Israel broke. This time the law will be written on their hearts, all will know him, and he will remember their sins no more. ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ spoke of the new covenant in his blood at the Last Supper, and the letter to the Hebrews quotes this passage at length.
32:
Now comes a dated narrative, set at the darkest point of all: the tenth year of ⟦p:zedekiah_1950|Zedekiah⟧, the eighteenth of ⟦p:nebuchadnezzar_2167|Nebuchadnezzar⟧. The Babylonian army is besieging ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧, and ⟦p:jeremiah_853|Jeremiah⟧ is confined in the courtyard of the guard at the palace, imprisoned by the king for saying that the city will fall.

His cousin Hanamel arrives from ⟦l:anathoth_63|Anathoth⟧ and asks him to buy the family field there. Under the law, when land had to be sold, the nearest kinsman had the right to buy it and keep it in the family. This land lies behind enemy lines, and its value must have seemed close to nothing.

Here we meet by name, for the first time, ⟦p:baruch_410|Baruch⟧ son of ⟦p:neriah_2186|Neriah⟧, ⟦p:jeremiah_853|Jeremiah⟧'s scribe. The purchase is done with legal care: silver weighed, the deed signed, sealed and witnessed, and two copies stored in a clay jar to last a long time. Then Jeremiah prays, and his prayer is honest about how strange it all seems. The Lord's answer is that nothing is too hard for him. The city will fall, and yet fields will be bought in this land again.
33:
⟦p:jeremiah_853|Jeremiah⟧ is still shut up in the courtyard of the guard when the word of the Lord comes to him a second time. Call to me, the Lord says, and I will answer you and show you great and hidden things.

The present is not softened. Houses in ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧, royal buildings among them, are being pulled down to shore up the walls against the siege ramps, and the gaps will be filled with the dead. Yet the Lord promises healing for this very city. In the empty streets, the sounds silenced in so many earlier chapters will be heard again: the voices of bride and bridegroom, and worshippers bringing thank offerings and singing that the Lord is good, his loving devotion endures forever. Shepherds will count their flocks again in the towns of Judah.

The righteous Branch of chapter twenty-three returns, and this time ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧ itself bears the name The Lord Our Righteousness. The last verses bind the covenant with ⟦p:david_994|David⟧ and with the Levitical priests to the fixed order of day and night. People are saying the Lord has rejected both Israel and Judah. He would sooner break his covenant with the sun and moon.
34:
We remain in the final siege. ⟦p:nebuchadnezzar_2167|Nebuchadnezzar⟧'s army, swelled with troops from the kingdoms under his control, is fighting against ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧, and only two other fortified towns of Judah still hold out, ⟦l:lachish_711|Lachish⟧ and ⟦l:azekah_128|Azekah⟧, in the lowlands to the south-west. Archaeologists at Lachish found letters written on broken pottery by Judean officers from about this time, and one reports that the signals from Azekah can no longer be seen.

⟦p:jeremiah_853|Jeremiah⟧ brings ⟦p:zedekiah_1950|Zedekiah⟧ a personal word. The city will burn, and the king will meet the king of ⟦l:babylon_151|Babylon⟧ face to face. Yet he will not die by the sword.

The rest of the chapter records a broken promise. ⟦p:zedekiah_1950|Zedekiah⟧ and the people had made a solemn covenant in the temple to free their Hebrew slaves, as the law of ⟦p:moses_2108|Moses⟧ required after six years of service. They did it, and then took the slaves back when the Babylonian army withdrew for a time and the danger seemed past. The covenant had been sealed by walking between the halves of a slaughtered calf. The fate of the calf, the Lord says, will now be theirs.
35:
This chapter steps back to the days of ⟦p:jehoiakim_1085|Jehoiakim⟧, when ⟦p:nebuchadnezzar_2167|Nebuchadnezzar⟧ had marched into the land and Chaldean and Aramean armies were roaming the countryside. Among those who have taken refuge inside ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧ is an unusual clan, the Rechabites.

They trace their customs to ⟦p:jonadab_799|Jonadab⟧ son of ⟦p:rechab_2403|Rechab⟧, who appears in the second book of Kings as an ally of King ⟦p:jehu_817|Jehu⟧, some two and a half centuries earlier. He commanded his descendants never to drink wine, build houses, sow fields or plant vineyards, but to live in tents. They have kept those rules ever since, and only the invasion has driven them into the city.

⟦p:jeremiah_853|Jeremiah⟧ brings the family into a room in the temple, sets bowls of wine and cups in front of them, and invites them to drink. They refuse, politely and firmly. The test is not a trap. It is a lesson staged for ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧. A family has kept the command of a human ancestor for generations, while Judah has not listened to the Lord, who has spoken again and again. The family receives a promise of its own.
36:
We go back to the fourth year of ⟦p:jehoiakim_1085|Jehoiakim⟧, the year of Carchemish. ⟦p:jeremiah_853|Jeremiah⟧ is told to write on a scroll everything the Lord has said to him since the days of ⟦p:josiah_1730|Josiah⟧. If the people hear the whole of it at once, each of them may yet turn from his wicked way and be forgiven.

⟦p:jeremiah_853|Jeremiah⟧ dictates and ⟦p:baruch_410|Baruch⟧ writes. Jeremiah himself is barred from the temple, so Baruch reads the scroll aloud there on a fast day the following year, from the room of ⟦p:gemariah_1296|Gemariah⟧ son of ⟦p:shaphan_2550|Shaphan⟧. Gemariah's son reports it to the royal officials, and they summon Baruch to read it to them too. Among them is Elnathan son of Achbor, the man who once fetched the prophet ⟦p:uriah_2898|Uriah⟧ back from ⟦l:egypt_362|Egypt⟧ to his death.

The officials are afraid. They tell ⟦p:baruch_410|Baruch⟧ and ⟦p:jeremiah_853|Jeremiah⟧ to hide, and take the scroll to the king. It is winter, and ⟦p:jehoiakim_1085|Jehoiakim⟧ is sitting in his winter apartment with a fire burning in a brazier in front of him. What he does next is one of the most vivid scenes in the book, and some of his own officials plead with him to stop. Then Jeremiah takes another scroll, and Baruch writes it all out again at his dictation, with many similar words added.
37:
The story jumps forward again, to ⟦p:zedekiah_1950|Zedekiah⟧'s reign and the siege. The chapter opens with a reminder of who Zedekiah is: placed on the throne by ⟦p:nebuchadnezzar_2167|Nebuchadnezzar⟧, and like those before him, not listening to the word of the Lord. Yet he keeps sending to ⟦p:jeremiah_853|Jeremiah⟧.

This scene comes earlier in the siege than the courtyard chapters we have just heard, and ⟦p:jeremiah_853|Jeremiah⟧ is still free to come and go. An Egyptian army has marched out to help Judah, and the Babylonians have lifted the siege to meet it. Hope revives in ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧. Jeremiah says it will not last. Even if the Babylonians were reduced to wounded men lying in their tents, they would rise up and burn the city.

During the lull, ⟦p:jeremiah_853|Jeremiah⟧ sets out for the land of ⟦p:benjamin_463|Benjamin⟧ to see to family property, and at the city gate he is arrested as a deserter. The officials beat him and shut him in a dungeon cell in the house of ⟦p:jonathan_1692|Jonathan⟧ the scribe for many days. Then the king sends for him in secret and asks a question he will ask more than once: is there any word from the Lord?
38:
In the courtyard of the guard, ⟦p:jeremiah_853|Jeremiah⟧ is still speaking to those around him, and his message has not changed. Whoever stays in the city will die. Whoever goes out to the Chaldeans will live. To a group of royal officials, among them ⟦p:pashur_2283|Pashhur⟧ son of Malchijah, this is treason, weakening the hands of the soldiers, and they demand his death.

⟦p:zedekiah_1950|Zedekiah⟧'s reply reveals the kind of king he is. He is in your hands, he says, for the king can do nothing against you. So ⟦p:jeremiah_853|Jeremiah⟧ is lowered by ropes into a cistern with no water in it, and sinks into the mud at the bottom.

Help comes from an unexpected quarter. ⟦p:ebed-melech_1029|Ebed-melech⟧, a Cushite from the kingdom on the upper ⟦l:nile_895|Nile⟧ beyond ⟦l:egypt_362|Egypt⟧, is an official in the palace, and he goes to the king to plead for the prophet. The rescue is told with tender detail. Then ⟦p:zedekiah_1950|Zedekiah⟧ meets ⟦p:jeremiah_853|Jeremiah⟧ secretly at an entrance to the temple. It is their last recorded conversation, and it shows a king afraid of almost everyone: the Babylonians, his own officials, and the Judeans who have already deserted.
39:
The siege comes to its end, told briefly and with dates. ⟦p:nebuchadnezzar_2167|Nebuchadnezzar⟧'s army arrived in the ninth year of ⟦p:zedekiah_1950|Zedekiah⟧, in the tenth month. In the eleventh year, on the ninth day of the fourth month, a year and a half later, the wall was broken through. The second book of Kings records the same events, and chapter fifty-two will tell them again.

Babylonian officers take their seats in the Middle Gate, a sign that the city now belongs to them. ⟦p:zedekiah_1950|Zedekiah⟧ and his soldiers slip out by night through the gate between the two walls by the king's garden and run east toward the ⟦l:jordan_653|Jordan⟧ valley. They are caught on the plains of ⟦l:jericho_634|Jericho⟧ and brought north to ⟦p:nebuchadnezzar_2167|Nebuchadnezzar⟧'s headquarters at ⟦l:riblah_1001|Riblah⟧, in ⟦l:syria_1122|Syria⟧. What happens to Zedekiah there is what ⟦p:jeremiah_853|Jeremiah⟧ had warned him of.

The palace and houses are burned and the walls pulled down. ⟦p:nebuzar-adan_2169|Nebuzaradan⟧, the captain of the guard, takes the people into exile and leaves only the poorest to work the land. By ⟦p:nebuchadnezzar_2167|Nebuchadnezzar⟧'s own order, ⟦p:jeremiah_853|Jeremiah⟧ is treated with care and entrusted to ⟦p:gedaliah_1287|Gedaliah⟧, grandson of ⟦p:shaphan_2550|Shaphan⟧. Last of all comes an earlier promise to ⟦p:ebed-melech_1029|Ebed-melech⟧, the man who pulled him out of the mud.
40:
⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧ has fallen, and the book follows the remnant left in Judah. First it fills in a detail. In the confusion after the city's capture, ⟦p:jeremiah_853|Jeremiah⟧ was caught up among the captives and taken in chains to ⟦l:ramah_972|Ramah⟧, the assembly point north of Jerusalem for those being sent to ⟦l:babylon_151|Babylon⟧. There ⟦p:nebuzar-adan_2169|Nebuzaradan⟧ sets him free, and even speaks of the disaster as the judgement of Jeremiah's God. He offers a choice: come to Babylon under his protection, or stay. Jeremiah stays.

⟦p:nebuchadnezzar_2167|Nebuchadnezzar⟧ has made ⟦p:gedaliah_1287|Gedaliah⟧ son of ⟦p:ahikam_141|Ahikam⟧ governor of what is left of Judah, with his seat at ⟦l:mizpah_811|Mizpah⟧, a few miles north of the ruined city. Army officers who had scattered into the countryside come to him, and Judeans who had fled to ⟦l:moab_815|Moab⟧, ⟦l:ammon_58|Ammon⟧ and ⟦l:edom_357|Edom⟧ begin to return. Gedaliah's advice is ⟦p:jeremiah_853|Jeremiah⟧'s: serve the king of ⟦l:babylon_151|Babylon⟧ and it will go well with you. That summer brings a rich harvest of grapes and fruit.

But one of the officers, ⟦p:johanan_1666|Johanan⟧ son of ⟦p:kareah_919|Kareah⟧, warns ⟦p:gedaliah_1287|Gedaliah⟧ that the king of the ⟦l:ammon_58|Ammonites⟧ has sent another, ⟦p:ishmael_631|Ishmael⟧ son of ⟦p:nethaniah_2198|Nethaniah⟧, to kill him. Gedaliah refuses to believe it.
41:
The warning proves true. In the seventh month, ⟦p:ishmael_631|Ishmael⟧ son of ⟦p:nethaniah_2198|Nethaniah⟧, a man of the royal family and one of the king's chief officers, comes to ⟦l:mizpah_811|Mizpah⟧ with ten men, and they sit down to a meal with the governor.

What follows is told without comment, and its violence spreads beyond ⟦p:gedaliah_1287|Gedaliah⟧: to the Judeans and Babylonian soldiers with him, and then to a group of pilgrims from ⟦l:shechem_1069|Shechem⟧, ⟦l:shiloh_1081|Shiloh⟧ and ⟦l:samaria_1022|Samaria⟧, coming in mourning, with offerings for the house of the Lord, unaware of what has happened. The cistern they end in was dug centuries earlier by King ⟦p:asa_318|Asa⟧.

⟦p:johanan_1666|Johanan⟧ and the other officers pursue ⟦p:ishmael_631|Ishmael⟧ and overtake him at the great pool of ⟦l:gibeon_470|Gibeon⟧. The captives are freed, though Ishmael escapes to ⟦l:ammon_58|Ammon⟧. Now the survivors are afraid. The man ⟦l:babylon_151|Babylon⟧ appointed has been murdered, and they expect reprisals. They stop near ⟦l:bethlehem_218|Bethlehem⟧, already meaning to go down to ⟦l:egypt_362|Egypt⟧. Jews have long kept a fast in the seventh month in memory of ⟦p:gedaliah_1287|Gedaliah⟧.
42:
The survivors are camped near ⟦l:bethlehem_218|Bethlehem⟧, on the road south. Before going further, the officers, with ⟦p:johanan_1666|Johanan⟧ son of ⟦p:kareah_919|Kareah⟧ at their head, come to ⟦p:jeremiah_853|Jeremiah⟧ with every appearance of humility. Pray to the Lord your God for us, they say, that he will show us the way to go. Whatever the answer, pleasant or unpleasant, we will obey.

⟦p:jeremiah_853|Jeremiah⟧ agrees, and then he waits. For ten days there is no answer. It is a small detail, but it says something about how the word came to him. He did not produce it on demand.

When the answer comes, it is clear. If they stay in the land, the Lord will build them up and not tear them down, plant them and not uproot them, the language of ⟦p:jeremiah_853|Jeremiah⟧'s first call. They need not fear the king of ⟦l:babylon_151|Babylon⟧. But if they go to ⟦l:egypt_362|Egypt⟧, looking for a land with no war, no trumpet and no hunger, the sword and famine they are fleeing will follow them there. Before he finishes, Jeremiah senses that their minds are already made up.
43:
The answer comes at once. ⟦p:johanan_1666|Johanan⟧, Azariah and the men with them call ⟦p:jeremiah_853|Jeremiah⟧ a liar. The Lord has not sent you, they say, and they blame ⟦p:baruch_410|Baruch⟧ for turning him against them so that they will be handed to the Babylonians.

So the whole remnant sets off for ⟦l:egypt_362|Egypt⟧: soldiers, women and children, the king's daughters, those who had come back from neighbouring lands, and ⟦p:jeremiah_853|Jeremiah⟧ and ⟦p:baruch_410|Baruch⟧ with them, against their will. They come to ⟦l:tahpanhes_1133|Tahpanhes⟧, a frontier town on the eastern edge of the ⟦l:nile_895|Nile⟧ Delta, where ⟦p:pharaoh_2336|Pharaoh⟧ had a residence.

⟦p:jeremiah_853|Jeremiah⟧'s ministry continues on foreign soil. As his fellow Judeans watch, he buries large stones in the brick pavement at the entrance to the royal building. ⟦p:nebuchadnezzar_2167|Nebuchadnezzar⟧, he says, will one day set his throne on these very stones. ⟦l:egypt_362|Egypt⟧, where they hoped to escape ⟦l:babylon_151|Babylon⟧, will feel its power too, and the obelisks of the temple of the sun, at the city the Greeks called Heliopolis, will be broken. A Babylonian inscription records that Nebuchadnezzar did campaign against Egypt years later.
44:
Some time has passed. Judeans are now living in several parts of ⟦l:egypt_362|Egypt⟧: at ⟦l:migdol_799|Migdol⟧ and ⟦l:tahpanhes_1133|Tahpanhes⟧ in the Delta, at ⟦l:memphis_779|Memphis⟧, the ancient capital near modern Cairo, and in ⟦l:pathros_925|Pathros⟧, the region of Upper Egypt to the south. ⟦p:jeremiah_853|Jeremiah⟧ addresses them all. It is the last of his messages that the book records.

He reminds them of what they have seen with their own eyes, the ruins of ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧ and the towns of Judah, and why it happened. Now in ⟦l:egypt_362|Egypt⟧ they are doing the same things again.

What makes the chapter unforgettable is the reply. A great crowd, men and women together, tell ⟦p:jeremiah_853|Jeremiah⟧ plainly that they will go on making offerings to the Queen of Heaven, as their fathers and kings did. Back then, they say, there was plenty of food and no disaster. It was when they stopped that everything went wrong. It is a rival reading of the same history. Jeremiah answers with a sign: ⟦p:pharaoh_2336|Pharaoh Hophra⟧ will be handed over to his enemies, as ⟦p:zedekiah_1950|Zedekiah⟧ was. Egyptian and Greek sources tell us that Hophra did lose his throne and his life in an uprising some years later.
45:
This short chapter is a postscript, and it takes us back some twenty years, to the fourth year of ⟦p:jehoiakim_1085|Jehoiakim⟧, when ⟦p:baruch_410|Baruch⟧ first wrote ⟦p:jeremiah_853|Jeremiah⟧'s words on a scroll.
